dataset.name: Untargeted metabolite data from a root surface in a rhizobox
description: Raw data is provided from samples analyzed using separate reverse phase chromatographic methods on a high performance liquid chromatograph with mass spectrometry. These porewater samples were collected from a microdialysis which generated samples along the surface of a growing A. sative root (all_hc). This data was used to answer questions connecting rhizosphere metabolite (putatively identified metabolites, hc_putative_norm) changes over time (root growth) with changes in the surrounding rhizosphere biogeochemistry (DOC, redox, pH). Rhizosphere biogeochemistry values are provided in the hc_putative_norm file as averages over their respective range of time that they were collected at. The hc_putative_norm file also contains all normalized values over only the intensity values collected for putatively identified metabolites.

measurementTechnique: Soils were brought to 40% water holding capacity using tap water and packed into the rhizobox to achieve a field bulk density (1.5 g cm−3). A single A. sativa seedling with a tap root of ∼4 cm length was transferred into the rhizobox. A. sativa was selected due to its significant agricultural value and the extensive research on its rhizosphere dynamics. Soil moisture was maintained using a cotton wick connected to an amber glass flask containing tap water placed along the side of the rhizobox. The polycarbonate portions of the rhizobox were covered with a aluminum foil to limit light exposure, leaving the top open for the plant to grow, and placed in a rack where it was held at a 30°-angle to facilitate plant root growth along the sensor array. Rhizoboxes were maintained in a growth chamber (Percival PGC-105HIDX, Percival Scientific, Perry, IA) set to a 16 h light and 8 h dark cycle with a maximum of 800 μmol photons m−2 s−1 at 20% humidity for light hour settings and 25 °C light cycle temperature and 15 °C dark cycle temperature. Plants were transitioning from seedling to vegetative stage by the time their roots arrived at the sensor array within the rhizoboxes. We determined the root growth rate by measuring the location of the root tip in relation to microsensors twice daily. Samples collected along the root were categorized into four groups depending on the location of the root tip and time elapsed: soil background, root tip zone, older root zone, and oldest root zone. Soil background was collected for 24 h before the root tip emerged alongside the sensor array. For statistical analyses, samples collected from the initial emergence of the root tip and through the subsequent 40 h were designated as the root tip zone, until the root tip had moved completely past the sensor array. Samples collected between 65 and 104 h from the start of the experiment, after the root tip had passed the sensor array, were designated as older root region, and samples collected between 105 and 124 h were designated as oldest root region. Rhizobox experiments were run in triplicates, microdialysis sampling was done every 4 h over the span of five consecutive days (i.e., 124 h).

Samples were analyzed using separate reverse phase chromatographic methods, while employing a porous graphite column (Thermo Hypercarb, 2.1 mm × 150 mm, 3 μm particles) at a flow rate of 200 μL min−1. Porewater samples (50 μL) were injected and separated using a gradient of ultrapure water +0.1% formic acid (solvent A) and acetonitrile +0.1% formic acid (solvent B), starting at 95:5% A/ B and ramping to 5:95% A/B over 30 min, followed by isocratic elution at 95% B for 5 min. Orbitrap MS data were collected in positive ionization mode from m/z 110−2000 with a resolving power of 120,000 at m/z 200. Tandem MS spectra with collision induced dissociation were collected in data dependent acquisition mode by using a collision energy of 35. An aligned metabolomic feature list was generated with MS-Dial (version 4.18) using a retention time tolerance of 0.5 min and MS tolerance of 0.015 Da. Putative metabolite identification of 15 molecules was based on MS/MS scoring to the MS-Dial MSMSPublic-Pos-VS15.msp library using an identification score cut off of 70%. Further putative identification was based on matching the exact mass of measured metabolites to the masses of genome-based metabolite predictions available for the related grass species Brachypodium from the PlantCyc plant metabolic network. Matched metabolites detected on the Hypercarb column were then grouped into compound classes such as “phenolic and organic acids,” “amino acids and derivatives,” “flavonoids and coumarins,” “sugars and derivatives,” “volatiles,” and if they did not fit in either of these classes they were placed under “other” in accordance with MS-Dial, PlantCyc Ontology, and PubChem classification systems. CSV file has all metabolites detected from HPLC MS using a hypercarb column from a rhizobox experiment where samples were collected as a root grew along a microdialysis probe
